name: Procyanidin B2
lead: Procyanidin B2 is a polyphenol from apples and other plants that is used in hair-growth tonics and supplements, with the aim of thicker, fuller hair. It is a B-type dimer of the procyanidin group of proanthocyanidins, built from catechin and epicatechin units; apples are a notable dietary source [1]. Hair-loss communities discuss it as a topical alternative or add-on to standard treatments.

Research on its hair effects traces to a Japanese group that studied apple procyanidins in cultured mouse hair cells and in mice. A 1999 Journal of Investigative Dermatology study reported that procyanidin B-2 raised growth of mouse hair epithelial cells to about 300% of control in vitro, and that a 1% topical application on shaved mice gave hair regeneration of 69.6% versus 41.7% for vehicle [2]. A 2000 double-blind trial in 29 men (19 on a 1% procyanidin B-2 tonic, 10 on placebo) reported a larger rise in total and terminal hair count than placebo over six months, with no adverse effects observed [2].

Later work looked at an Annurca apple formulation rich in procyanidin B2, reported in a 2018 randomized clinical trial [3]. Broader reviews cover procyanidin B2 as a food-derived pigment with many studied bioactivities, mostly outside hair [4].

paras: Procyanidins are condensed flavan-3-ols. Wikipedia lists procyanidin B2 among B-type dimers; apples contain roughly 70-141 mg proanthocyanidins per 100 g, with some of the highest levels in Red Delicious and Granny Smith varieties. [1]

A 1999 Journal of Investigative Dermatology paper reported that procyanidin oligomers, procyanidin B-2 among them, selectively promoted mouse hair epithelial cell growth in vitro and activated hair follicle growth in mice [2]. A 2000 Skin Pharmacology paper found that selective protein kinase C inhibitors including procyanidin B-2 and C-1 promoted epithelial cell growth and anagen induction, while procyanidins that also inhibited protein kinase A were less active [2]. A 2002 British Journal of Dermatology laboratory study reported that procyanidin B-2 reduced expression and translocation of several PKC isozymes, which the authors suggest partly explains the effect [2].

A 2006 study examined procyanidin oligomers against TGF-beta-induced apoptosis in murine hair epithelial cells and found that B-2 and B-3 counteracted it, with B-2 increasing MEK-1/2 expression [2]. A toxicology paper from 1999 reported B-2 was non-mutagenic in bacteria and the micronucleus test, caused no primary skin irritation in rabbits and no sensitisation in guinea pigs [2].

A 2012 randomized study titled 'Intake of dietary procyanidins does not contribute to the pool of circulating flavanols in humans' examined what happens to eaten procyanidins in the body [5]. The hair studies of the tonic involve topical application rather than oral intake [2].

Two reports from the same group describe a double-blind trial of 29 men, 19 using 1% procyanidin B-2 tonic and 10 placebo. The Phytomedicine 2000 paper reported total hair count rising by 6.68 per 0.25 cm2 with treatment versus 0.08 with placebo (P < 0.005) and terminal hair count rising by 1.99 versus a decline of 0.82 over six months [2]. The Phytotherapy Research 2001 paper reported that 78.9% of the treatment group had increased mean hair diameter versus 30.0% with placebo, and total hair count rose by 3.67 versus a decline of 2.54 over four months [2]. No adverse effects were observed in either group [2].

A 2018 Journal of Medicinal Food paper reports a randomized clinical trial of an Annurca apple nutraceutical on hair growth plus a human skin model; it tested an extract formulation rather than pure procyanidin B2 [3].

timeline.event: Mouse and in-vitro studies report procyanidin B-2 promotes hair follicle growth; toxicology study published [2].

card.summary: An apple polyphenol with early lab, mouse and small human data for hair growth, mostly using whole extracts.
card.note: Evidence is for extracts, not isolated B2.

quick.overview:
Procyanidin B2 is a polyphenol found in apples, promoted as a hair-growth ingredient.

Research includes cell studies, mouse studies and one randomized trial of an Annurca apple formulation.
quick.mechanism: Proposed actions include protecting hair epithelial cells from TGF-beta-induced apoptosis and boosting keratin expression. [2]
quick.risks: Dietary procyanidins are common in food; safety of concentrated supplements was not assessed in the sources reviewed.

chain: Topical or dietary procyanidin B2 from apple
Proposed action on hair epithelial cells and follicle growth phase
Higher hair counts and thicker hair
angle.text: People apply apple-procyanidin tonics or take apple-extract supplements hoping for denser hair. Small human trials of a 1% topical tonic reported greater hair counts than placebo.
